story.title: India's Youth-Led 'Cockroach' Protests Force Modi Government's Rare Capitulation
story.summary: Gen Z protesters in India, using the cockroach metaphor, forced the resignation of the education minister over exam standard concerns, marking a rare public retreat by PM Modi.

rows.title: Dharmendra Pradhan, CJP: India's 'cockroach' protest called off after education minister quits - BBC News
rows.text:
India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has called off its five-week-long protest, hours after Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned.

The CJP has called it a win for democracy and thousands of jubilant supporters continue to celebrate at Jantar Mantar, the main protest venue in Delhi.

An online satirical campaign with an AI-generated cockroach as its mascot, the CJP is not a real party but has evolved into a powerful platform for young people's anxieties and dissent.

The protest has been the most visible expression of public anger against PM Narendra Modi's government in recent years and gained momentum after Monday's police crackdown on people marching to parliament left dozens injured .

Pradhan announced his resignation on X in a post in Hindi saying he "respected the aspirations, dreams, and expectations of the youth" and was "pained by the events" of the past few days.

"Considering the situation at Jantar Mantar and across the country - with the aim of preventing anti-national forces from exploiting it, preserving national unity, ensuring that not a single Indian student's future gets entangled in legal complexities, and allowing our children to devote their time to studies and focus on building their careers - I have submitted my resignation to the prime minister," he wrote.

As news of Pradhan's resignation broke, a visibly emotional Abhijeet Dipke, CJP's founder, screamed from the makeshift stage at Jantar Mantar: "We have done it."

A loud cheer went up and huge celebrations erupted with the protesters singing, dancing, shouting slogans and handing out sweets.

Several hours since the CJP announced the end of their protest and its leaders left the site, crowds were still gathered at the venue into the night.

Many told the BBC they had waited for this day for weeks, and were not in the mood to leave without celebrating.

The site is increasingly looking like the centre of a party, with volunteers doing their best to manage the crowds. A large number of police are deployed around the area, but they say they will intervene only if they see breaches of the law.

The CJP was formed after the chief justice of India described some unemployed young people turning to journalism and activism as "cockroaches". He later said he was referring specifically to people with "fake and bogus degrees", but by then, the term had taken a life on its own.

The movement is led by Abhijeet Dipke, a 30-year-old political communications strategist and former student at Boston University.

The CJP quickly gained a huge following online, turning one of the most reviled insects into a symbol of defiance and resilience with 26 million followers on Instagram.

It called for reforms to India's education system, greater accountability over exam paper leaks and the resignation of Pradhan.

The protests gained global attention after activist and educationist Sonam Wangchuk joined them on 28 June and began an indefinite hunger strike in support of their demands.

As his health deteriorated, the crowds began to swell and Wangchuk was forcibly removed from the protest site by the police last Saturday and taken to hospital where he continued to fast. He finally called it off early Friday morning following assurances from the government that his demands would be looked into.

Over the course of the protest, most of India's major opposition political parties, activists and many celebrities turned up to show solidarity.

On the ground at the protest sites, many of the posters and slogans were directed at Modi.

The BBC met several people who said they had once supported the prime minister but had now turned against him.

"I used to support him when he used to do good things, but slowly I am realised that he is only dividing people on the basis of religion, and he's not doing anything else," said Radhika.

On Saturday, opposition leaders welcomed Pradhan's resignation, with many calling it a victory for the youth-led movement.

While the demand was for the resignation of the education minister, it is clear that the protests have dealt a severe blow to the prime minister's personal brand, and his aura of invincibility.

Since coming to power in 2014, Modi's government has rarely tolerated dissent and cracked down heavily on protests, which is why Pradhan's resignation is being seen as a big deal in India.

But this isn't the first time they have faced big protests - and it's not the first time they been forced into a climbdown either. Back in 2021, the government repealed agriculture laws after a year-long protest by farmers.

The students' protest has resonated with a large section of middle-class India, cutting across identities of religion, caste or sectors, with people voicing anger about the lack of educational opportunities and jobs in India.

Pressure grew on the government after Monday's violent crackdown when police and paramilitary forces used batons and wooden sticks to beat up young men and women, firing tear gas cans at them.

About 300 people were taken to hospital. Police said at least half of the injured were security personnel and also arrested about 70 protesters - most of them have since been released on bail.

After ignoring the protesters for nearly five weeks, Modi finally broke his silence on Thursday to say they had "decided to set up fast-track courts to ensure swift and stringent punishment for those involved in paper leaks".

And later that night, Modi posted a video message saying that a tough new law on examination paper leaks was being prepared. He said he had received a draft of the law, which they wanted to introduce soon in parliament.

Thousands of posts mocking Modi have flooded social media. The prime minister's videos, intended to quell anger, have been turned into jokes and memes.

Following Pradhan's resignation, the CJP founder Dipke said in a statement on X that the fight was not over yet.

He said they would continue to fight for the families of students who died by suicide after a key medical exam was cancelled to ensure they received compensation.

He also renewed his calls for action against police officers he accused of using excessive force against protesters on 20 July on CJP supporters who tried to march to Parliament.

"Remember, do not mess with [the] cockroach," he added.

rows.title: WATCH: What to know about India's youth-led Gen Z 'cockroach' protests | PBS News
rows.text:
Zeba Warsi Zeba Warsi

Why are tens of thousands of young Indians suddenly calling themselves cockroaches?

What began as outrage over leaked national entrance exams has exploded into one of India's biggest youth-led protest movements in years. It's a direct challenge from Gen Z to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and it's spreading to cities across India despite a government crackdown.

Here's what to know.

It began with an insult. After India's chief justice compared unemployed young people to "cockroaches" during a court hearing, students adopted the label.

Boston University graduate student Abhijeet Dipke posted on X "What if all Cockroaches come together." Within hours, he created a website and social media pages for the "Cockroach Janata Party" or CJP, a satirical take on Modi's ruling BJP.

The CJP Instagram page has amassed more than 25 million followers, more than twice that of BJP.

The outrage over the 'cockroach' insult came after India's Ministry of Education threw out the results of an entrance exam for undergraduate medical programs because questions on the test had been leaked in advance. Two million students had already taken the costly and difficult test, and news that it wouldn't count sparked outrage.

India's hyper-competitive entrance exams can determine the future for millions of students and offer a means of upward social mobility.

Repeated allegations of leaks and corruption left many students feeling their years of hard work had disappeared overnight. Activists have linked the leak to at least 20 student deaths by suicide, according to the Times of India.

Among other things, protesters are demanding the ouster of India's education minister, increased punishments for people who leak test materials and fee compensation when exams are voided.

Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.

A broader list on the party's website is also pushing for increased representation of women in parliament, a more independent media system and the arrest of the chief election commissioner if votes are ever erased.

These are part of a push for more accountability, not just for exam failures, but for what they see as a political system that has failed young people.

Clashes broke out this week as CJP protesters marched toward India's Parliament. Demonstrators accused law enforcement of using excessive force as they targeted unarmed students with tear gas, batons and reportedly even pellet guns. But if the goal was to break the movement, it appears to have had the opposite effect.

"If the government thinks that doing this with Gen Z can stop us, then that won't happen," student Sona Bisht, 20, told the Associated Press. "We are here talking about education, talking about securing our future. And till the time our demands are not met, we will not move from here."

And as the Gen Z supporters of the CPJ movement document arrests in real time and use memes and humor to challenge the government, people across India have shown their support by sending meals and supplies to students camped at protest sites through food delivery apps.

WATCH: India's Muslims continue to face discrimination and hate following Modi's election win

India's Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi and other opposition leaders have backed the demonstrations, accusing the government of failing India's youth.

Government supporters and some mainstream media outlets, meanwhile, have portrayed the protesters as anarchist and influenced by foreign actors.

"This idea that anyone who is critical of any aspect of the government is anti-national or is a terrorist, I think there's an exhaustion with that discourse, an anger at that discourse that genuine legitimate criticism is reframed as being anti- national — that being critical of Mr. Modi is somehow being anti-Indian," said Rohit Chopra, a professor of communication at Santa Clara University and visiting fellow at the Center for South Asia at Stanford University.

Modi broke his silence Wednesday after weeks of protests, announcing fast-track judicial measures to address the exam scandal. But he stopped short of dismissing the education minister, one of the protesters' central demands.

A sign is seen during a July 20 demonstration in Kolkata, India, in solidarity with protests by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) held at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi. Photo by Sahiba Chawdhary/Reuters.

India has seen major protests before. But analysts say this moment feels different. This isn't just a protest against a policy. It's now challenging the authority of three-time Prime Minister Narendra Modi himself, Chopra said.

"I've seen lots of posters and songs in different idioms, whether it's sort of rap or poetry, basically mocking Mr. Modi. What is different right now is the fact that this brutality is linked and seen as the responsibility of the Prime Minister directly and protesters are very unequivocally asking for accountability from the Prime minister, Mr. Modi, himself," Chopra said.

"No matter what the immediate consequence or outcome of these protests, whether [the education minister] resigns, whether there is some kind of reform in this whole examination system, all of that remains to be seen. But I think one thing is for certain, the aura surrounding Mr. Modi has been damaged permanently."

Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.

Zeba Warsi Zeba Warsi

Zeba Warsi is a foreign affairs producer, based in Washington DC. She's a Columbia Journalism School graduate with an M.A. in Political journalism. She was one of the leading members of the NewsHour team that won the 2024 Peabody award for News for our coverage of the war in Gaza and Israel.

rows.title: briefing 2026-07-25
rows.text:
# NewsLens — Saturday, July 25, 2026

In today's briefing:
- Iran reports first strike-free night in 13 as Saudi-Houthi front opens
- India's Gen Z 'cockroach' movement forces education minister to quit
- Energy Department concedes it cut blue-state grants for their politics
- Paramount pauses Warner Bros. Discovery close until court rules
- New Trump tariffs hit 60 trading partners as legal fight opens
- Zelensky fights to contain fallout as Drapatyi takes top command
- West Bank shooting kills six as Israel arrests dozens of Palestinians

---
**Iran reports first strike-free night in 13 as Saudi-Houthi front opens**

Iran's health ministry reported Saturday the first night in 13 without a US strike, after nearly two weeks of Central Command hitting Iranian command centers, drone stores and coastal surveillance. A second front opened as the first went quiet: the Houthis claimed missile attacks on two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea and a strike on the Saudi city of Jizan that set off fires, and the Saudi-led coalition hit Houthi positions in Yemen's Hodeida port and a nearby island. US forces fired on the merchant vessel M/T Lavine in the Gulf of Oman after it tried at least four times to breach the blockade of Iranian ports. Brent crude briefly topped $100 a barrel this week for the first time in two months, and only one tanker crossed the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday — the fewest since May 7, per Kpler tracking. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, accused Washington of forcing open a Hormuz route that bypasses Iranian authority in breach of the June US-Iran memorandum, even as both sides confirmed talks continue.

**Why it matters:** This is the resumed campaign that abandoned the July 16 ceasefire and widened from military targets to civilian water and power — the July 18 strike on a desalination plant serving 20 Iranian villages. Brent first broke $90 on July 20; this week it cleared $100. Human costs have mounted: at least 18 American service members killed and more than 3,400 dead per Iran's health ministry since the Feb. 28 joint US-Israeli strikes that opened the war. The conflict now runs on two live fronts at once: the core US-Iran exchange and a fresh Saudi-Houthi clash over Red Sea shipping. The Houthis, whom Trump calls Iran's proxy, opened that second front, and the firing on the M/T Lavine shows the US blockade of Iranian ports now reaching into the Gulf of Oman — so Saturday's pause with Iran, even if it holds, doesn't prevent the broader conflict from spreading. Trump framed the endgame as a binary — 'knocking out everything they have' or a negotiated deal — and declined to say whether destroying Iranian bridges or power plants would be a war crime; strikes on civilian-serving infrastructure risk that classification under the Geneva Conventions absent a definite military advantage. Oman, which controls the strait's southern coast, is mediating the transit dispute Araghchi says Washington is bypassing. At home, the House passed a war-powers resolution and the Senate failed to advance a binding version, so no legal constraint now limits the campaign — its continuation sits with Trump alone. Analysts doubt escalation works: Sina Azodi of George Washington University argues intensifying strikes won't change Iran's calculus because Tehran treats the war as existential, and former defense secretary Leon Panetta calls it a slide toward a Vietnam-style forever war with the US 'in deep trouble.' The cost is landing at home too — the 30-year mortgage rate rose to 6.85% Thursday, its highest since June 2025, the 10-year Treasury yield neared 4.7%, and gas averages about $4.10 a gallon.

**Watch for:** Whether Central Command reports fresh strikes in the nights after July 25 settles whether Saturday's quiet is a durable lull or a reload — and the tempo determines whether the Oman-mediated Hormuz talks proceed or collapse as they did in early July. The US and UK are planning an international conference on the strait

rows.text:
# NewsLens — Friday, July 24, 2026

In today's briefing:
- Oil tops $100 as attacks strike Red Sea, Hormuz and Black Sea
- Israel deploys troops across West Bank after deadly Tal shooting
- Russian missiles kill 10 near Kyiv as Ukraine strikes deep
- Paramount freezes $111bn Warner Bros deal as states' antitrust suit proceeds
- OpenAI agent ran undetected in Hugging Face systems for a week
- US and Iran trade strikes as Trump weighs bigger offensive
- Trump hits 60 trading partners with new tariffs; businesses sue

---
**Oil tops $100 as attacks strike Red Sea, Hormuz and Black Sea**

Brent crude broke $100 a barrel Thursday for the first time since May, after Yemen's Houthis claimed attacks on two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea — strikes they had preceded by declaring a maritime embargo against Riyadh, opening a second front alongside Iran's campaign in the Strait of Hormuz. (CBS put Thursday's peak slightly lower, at $98.82.) By Friday the price had given most of it back, falling nearly 4% to close at $96.78, with WTI down 3% at $89.31, after Reuters reported that Pakistan — with China's backing — is pushing to restart US-Iran talks. A third artery closed at the same time: Russia's largest Black Sea export terminal, Sheskharis at Novorossiysk, has loaded no crude since July 21, after Ukrainian drone strikes that also shut the CPC terminal. US Central Command completed its 13th consecutive night of strikes on Iran, targeting military command centres, drone storage and coastal surveillance.

**Why markets care:** Brent first cracked $90 on Jul 20, the day the Houthis declared their naval blockade of Saudi Arabia; four days later that declaration hardened into strikes on two actual Saudi tankers, and the price cleared $100. What separates this from a single-chokepoint scare is that three arteries are constricting at once — Iran hitting vessels in Hormuz, the Houthis firing on Saudi tankers in the Red Sea after embargoing Riyadh, and Ukrainian drones, which Kyiv says have now struck more than 150 shadow-fleet vessels in the Black and Azov seas, idling Russia's largest export terminal. Commodity strategist Helima Croft said the market is now pricing wars on multiple fronts at once rather than one regional disruption. The squeeze lands precisely on Saudi Arabia's insurance against a Hormuz closure — the East-West pipeline that reroutes crude to Yanbu on the Red Sea — and those Yanbu loadings had already fallen 41% since March, to about 2.39 million barrels a day by June, before the Houthis started targeting Saudi tankers at all. That is the reversal at the story's core: the bypass built to survive a Hormuz shutdown is now itself the thing under attack. The deeper worry traders described is structural: with Hormuz, the Red Sea's Bab el-Mandeb detour and now the Black Sea all under fire, the system has fewer paths to move barrels rather than one damaged chokepoint — every reroute the market was counting on is itself a target. Rapidan Energy Group expects Brent to hold near $100 through the end of 2026 as long as the ceasefire breakdown persists. Kpler's Matt Smith, director of commodity research, said the Red Sea attacks push any Hormuz reopening into next year. Prediction markets moved with him: Kalshi's odds that Hormuz traffic returns to normal by July 2027 fell to 47% from nearly 70% in two days, with the seven-day average of transit calls at about 12 against the 60 the contract needs to clear. Friday's near-4% pullback traced entirely to that one Reuters report of a diplomatic opening — not to any barrel actually moving — which is its own measure of how thin the cushion has become. Trump, in a Thursday Axios interview, said he would hold Iran responsible and signalled a further 'massive attack,' the escalation risk sitting directly opposite the Pakistan-brokered channel that pulled the price down. ---
**India's Gen Z 'cockroach' movement forces education minister to quit**

India's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, resigned Saturday, announcing it on X after talks with the Cockroach Janta Party — the youth movement that had built nationwide protests against him. The CJP called the protests off within hours, saying the government had met its demands: dropping police cases against protesters and compensating the families of students who died by suicide after the alleged exam-paper leak. The movement started when the ministry voided an undergraduate medical entrance exam after questions leaked, upending two million students who had already sat it. The movement took its name after India's chief justice compared unemployed young people to 'cockroaches' in a court hearing; a Boston University graduate student, Abhijeet Dipke, turned the insult into a parody party after posting 'What if all Cockroaches come together.' Activist Sonam Wangchuk ended a 26-day hunger strike on Thursday, down 11kg.

**The stakes:** The insult handed the movement a ready-made identity, and Dipke's parody party turned it into reach: the CJP's Instagram following tops 25 million, more than twice the BJP's, and its meme output out-published the ruling party's own channels. Wangchuk's hunger strike supplied the moral weight a purely online campaign lacks, and with tear-gassed crowds at Delhi's Jantar Mantar still growing, Pradhan traded his job — and the government its concessions — to make the protests stop. He framed the exit as necessary 'so that antinational forces do not take advantage of this situation,' after earlier calling the students a 'B-team of terrorists.' NPR assesses the movement as the biggest challenge to Modi's 12 years in power, with whether he can calm Gen Z anger the open question. Whether this stays a single-demand protest or becomes the front edge of a broader youth mobilization, as some earlier Indian student movements did, turns on whether the CJP's organizing outlives Wangchuk's fast and Pradhan's exit. The stakes for Modi: a digitally organized youth bloc just forced a cabinet resignation in the world's largest democracy without a party, an office, or a single election on the calendar.

**What would change this:** The test is whether the CJP registers as a formal party or fields candidates — its following becomes power only if channeled into candidacies rather than dispersed. Modi has yet to name a successor, and the CJP and ministers are due for further talks on the exam-reform review the government agreed to.

*Reported by 6 named outlets — Al Jazeera, BBC News — World, Financial Times, NBC News, NPR, PBS NewsHour. Here for: India Politics.*

---
**Energy Department concedes it cut blue-state grants for their politics**

The Energy Department conceded in a court filing that the 284 grants it terminated in an October 2025 tranche were selected 'based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient's state.' All but one of those grants tie to states that voted for Kamala Harris in 2024 and seat two Democratic-caucusing senators; 340 other grants DOE had flagged, in Trump-won or Republican-Senate states, were never canceled. The admission came from the department's principal deputy general counsel, Jeff Novak, responding to a lawsuit by University of California researchers challenging the cuts. OMB Director Russell Vought had announced the cancellations publicly as nearly $8 billion in green-energy funding, naming 15 states from California to New York.

**What changed:** What changed is the paper trail: DOE says it first assembled 624 grants for possible termination without regard to state politics, then OMB picked the 284 for October — and the concession surfaced through the candor a court filing demands, not a voluntary disclosure. In litigation terms, an undisputed statement of fact that the tranche was chosen on state politics hands the plaintiffs their central claim without their having to prove it. It also sits against the department's public line: Energy Secretary Chris Wright has testified the selection wasn't political, and a DOE spokesperson said his statements 'are still correct' — a direct conflict with the department's own filing on the same tranche. This is not the first blow: a federal judge already ruled related cuts unlawful for disproportionately hitting Democratic-led states, and the DOE inspector general has opened a probe into the roughly $8 billion. Congressional Democrats are demanding the withheld money be released now that the selection is conceded as political. And per NOTUS, the cuts weren't cleanly partisan — they also killed some red-state awards and bit into the administration's own stated energy priorities.

**The next test:** Whether the roughly $8 billion is released turns on DOE's next filing in the UC suit — comply or appeal — and the inspector general's report will show whether it recommends referral to watchdogs at other agencies, such as HHS's blue-state health grants.

*Reported by 2 named outlets (plus 1 wire-syndicated item(s), excluded from the count) — NBC News, The Hill. Here for: Policy Failure.*

---
**Paramount pauses Warner Bros. Discovery close until court rules**

Paramount told a federal court it won't close its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery until a judge rules on the merits of a 12-state antitrust lawsuit or June 1, 2027 — whichever comes first. Reports on the deal value conflict: Washington Times places it at $81 billion, Fox Business at $111 billion, versus $55 billion cited earlier. The states and the Writers Guild of America are seeking to block the merger outright.
